items.title: How Different are Different Differences-in-Differences? A Large-Scale Meta-Analysis
items.desc: Uses AI-assisted replication of 1,346 staggered-adoption specifications from 108 economics papers to show that two-way fixed effects estimates are highly correlated with modern DiD estimates (sign reversals in 10.8-14.5% of comparisons), suggesting negative weights matter less in practice. [arXiv econ.EM, submitted 2026-10-29]

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: This one is about a long-running worry in applied economics: whether the standard two-way fixed effects approach to difference-in-differences is badly biased. We're working from the abstract only.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: Right, the concern is negative weights, where some comparisons get counted backwards when treatment timing is staggered. Newer estimators fix that, but how much did it matter in real papers?

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: The author uses AI-assisted replication to rerun 1,346 staggered-adoption specifications drawn from 108 economics papers, comparing the old estimates with modern ones.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: And the headline is that they are highly correlated. Sign reversals show up in roughly eleven to fourteen and a half percent of comparisons, and the old approach is actually more precise.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Then a hierarchical model accounts for estimation noise. It implies a correlation of ninety-one to ninety-eight percent between the underlying estimands, and only a small chance, between point six and two point one percent, of getting a significant estimate with the wrong sign.

podcast.speaker: B
podcast.text: So the takeaway is that negative weights may be a less serious problem in practice than feared, and the paper also pitches AI as a way to run large-scale checks of new econometric methods.

podcast.speaker: A
podcast.text: Caveat, since we only have the abstract: the details of the replication pipeline matter, and we can't judge them here.
